title: Permeability: Darcy, Millidarcy and m²
h1: Rock and material permeability — darcy, millidarcy and m²
description: 1 darcy = 9.869 × 10⁻¹³ m². Reservoir sandstones are 10–1000 md; shales are <0.01 md. Pump curves and well design run on this factor.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 and category-specific ISO references

hero: Darcy is a geology unit; m² is SI. The 12-order-of-magnitude conversion is what separates a producing well from a plugged one.
body: Permeability is the property that turns Darcy's law into flow prediction. Reservoir engineers use darcys and millidarcys; SI-strict soil mechanics uses m². The conversion factor is small — small enough that memorising one figure saves an hour of unit hunting.

> 1 darcy = 9.869233 × 10⁻¹³ m² ≈ 10⁻¹² m²
> 1 md = 10⁻³ darcy ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ m²
High-quality reservoir sandstone: 100–1000 md. Tight gas: 0.1–10 md. Shale (matrix): <0.001 md. Concrete: ~10⁻¹⁹ m² (~0.1 nd). Coarse sand aquifer: 10–100 darcy.

A 100 md sandstone, 20 m thick, 200 cP viscosity, produces via Darcy: q = k A ΔP / (µ L). Drop k to 1 md (unaltered core → damaged near-well) and productivity falls 100×. Skin damage is a permeability unit conversation dressed up as a well-completion problem.
1 darcy ≈ 10⁻¹² m². Millidarcys are the working range for tight reservoirs.

faqs.q: Is permeability a fluid or rock property?
faqs.a: Intrinsic permeability is a rock property. Hydraulic conductivity multiplies it by ρg/µ, giving m/s — this depends on the fluid.
10⁻⁹ darcy ≈ 10⁻²¹ m². Used for source-rock shales.
